reader.title: Killing of an unidentified Black man at Cornfield Point, Louisiana
bases: The only source lists the case in a 'Record of Lynching' of men who 'lost their lives at the hands of a mob' in 1903, with no further detail (A2).
One entry in one Black-press tally reprinted from The Striker; no local, wire or other report of the killing was found in either press (A2).

summary.text: The killing of an unidentified Black man at Cornfield Point, Louisiana, was a mob killing listed as having taken place on January 19, 1903.
It is known only from a single line in a lynching tally that the Sedalia Times printed in August 1903, which gave no name, charge or circumstances.
The tally's January entries include the line "19—Unknown Negro, Cornfield Point, Lat," in which the state abbreviation is most likely a garbled "La."
Most other entries in the list name the victim and an alleged offense, such as "murder" or "assault," but this one gives neither.
No local or wire report of a killing at Cornfield Point appears in the coverage, and no inquest, arrest or other aftermath is reported.
The Sedalia Times ran the list on August 29, 1903, under the headline "Record of Lynching," crediting it to The Striker.

The paper introduced it as showing "how far mob violence has gone and at what a rapid pade [pace] it is going," counted 48 men killed by mobs up to July 1, and said the South alone had furnished 44 of them.
It described the killers as "lawless men," placing the Cornfield Point case among the year's mob killings rather than reporting it as a separate story.
No white-press account of a killing at Cornfield Point was found, so the case survives only as an entry in the Black press's running count of mob killings.

accounts.label: The Striker's lynching record (reprinted by the Sedalia Times)
accounts.gist: Lists an 'Unknown Negro' as lynched at Cornfield Point, Louisiana, on January 19, 1903, without a charge or details.

framing.detail: Under the headline 'Record of Lynching', the Sedalia Times introduced the list as showing 'how far mob violence has gone' and called the killers 'lawless men'.
